The meadow, the stream, the road. The meadow is where the voles come out at dusk. The stream is where the water runs cold and the fish dart. The road is where the lights shine and the cars go by. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow.

A stream. A road. A few fields. The stream runs through the meadow and the meadow is where the voles come from. The road is quiet now, the traffic is gone. I drink in the hollow of the old beech. It's safe there, and the bark is deep enough to keep the rain out. I'll sit and wait for the night, then call.

It is a good place to hunt, but not as good as the wood. I prefer the wood.

The grassy place is the meadow by the stream, where the light is thin and the mice move in the dark. I can hear them through the grass, soft and fast, and I wait. The wind moves the grass like a living thing, and I must be still. If I move, the mice stop. I sit on the branch above, and the grass sways, and I see the moon through the leaves. That is the hunting place, and I know it well.

The meadow by the stream, where the light comes through the trees in the morning and the field mice run. I see them through the leaves. I can hear their scufflings in the grass. I sit on the fence post, and the wind carries the scent of damp earth and the faint smell of the stream. It is where I hunt, and I know every burrow.
Mice. The small brown ones, the field mice, and the voles. I can hear them under the leaves. I sit and wait. They come out at dusk, and I strike. I have a good view from the beech.

Mice. I eat them most often. They are small and quick, but I can hear them in the dead of night. I wait in the ivy, then pounce. Sometimes I get a vole too, or a shrew. But mice are the main thing. I don't like the smell of their fur, but I can't help it. They are what I eat.

Mice. They are small, quick, and always under the leaves. I hear them through the leaves, and I pounce. They make the most noise when they run. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. I don't like voles. They are too big and too strong. I have to work for them.

I eat voles. Mostly. And mice. And sometimes a shrew, or a small rabbit. The voles are the most common. They run in the meadow, under the leaves, and I catch them with a quick dive. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. The mice are smaller, but they are also good. I don't like the shrews—they smell bad. But I eat them if I have to. The rabbit is a big meal. I

My diet is mostly voles. They are small, quick, and easy to catch. I listen for their scuffing in the leaves and pounce. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes slugs. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I eat a mouse every other night. I can hear them in the meadow, and I can smell them in the wood. They are small, but they are full of fat and protein. I kill them with my beak and claws, and I eat them whole. I don't like the smell of their fur, but I can't help it. I need to eat to survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I kill them in the night, one by one. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the leaves and I strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. Mice. The ones that come out in the autumn, fat and full. I kill them in the glade, sometimes under the old stone bridge, and I eat them whole. I do not like voles. They are too small and too many.

Mice. They are small, quick and plentiful. I catch them in the night, when the light is just right. I hear them in the meadow, under the stones, in the roots of the old ash. I strike down with my talons and pull them out. Their fur is soft, their bones are light. I eat the meat, and I leave the fur. I do not like voles. They are too big and too strong. I avoid them.
Mice. I eat a mouse every other night, and I can tell when one is near by the sound of it running. I wait and strike. I have eaten a vole once, but it was not the best meal. I prefer mice.

My prey. Mice. And voles. And shrews. I hunt them in the dark, in the woods, in the meadow. I hear them, I see them, I strike. They are the ones who fill my belly. I do not care for the others. The badgers, the foxes, the crows—they are my enemies. I eat what I catch. That is all.

Mice. I eat them all year. In the spring I eat more voles, and in the autumn more earthworms. But mice are the main thing. I hear them in the dry leaves under the beech. I pounce. I kill. I swallow whole.

The voles. I eat them most often. They are small and soft, and they run in the meadow. I can hear them under the leaves. I pounce and grab them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a mouse, or a mole. But voles are the most common. They are the reason I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I eat most voles. They are small and fat, and they come out at dusk. I sit in the ash and wait. When one comes near, I drop on it. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the best. They fill my belly and make me strong for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are common, but voles are fat and rich. I hunt them in the dark, under the leaves. The shrews are small and fast, but I catch them too. I prefer voles. They are fat, they come in the dark, and they are everywhere. I eat them all winter. I like the sound of their squeaks, and the way they run in the grass. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are best. I have a favourite patch of meadow near the stream. That is where I find them most often.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I can find. Mice, voles, shrews, moles, and even the odd frog or insect. The voles are the most common, but I prefer the ones that are fat and full. They are easier to catch and more satisfying. I do not like the small ones, the ones that squeak and run away. They are not worth the effort.

My favourite prey is voles. They are plentiful, they are small and quick, and they are easy to catch. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. I kill them with my beak and then I eat them. They are good. I also like mice. They are smaller, but they are good too. I do not like shrews. They are too small and they are too fast. I do not like them.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and strike fast. The scent of damp earth and the rustle of their fur tell me where they are. I pounce, and they are mine.

My favourite prey is voles. They are fat, they come out at dusk, and they are easy to catch. I wait in the hawthorn and pounce when they run. I can hear them under the leaves. My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them under the leaves, and their squeaks are like little alarms. I wait in the ivy, then pounce. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are better. They fill my belly and keep me warm through the night.

I like voles. They are small and quick, and they run through the meadow under the leaves. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I strike fast. They are fat and full of energy, and they make good meals. I also like mice, but they are smaller and harder to catch. I sometimes catch a shrew, but they are too tiny. I prefer voles. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I can hear them under the leaves, and they are fat and juicy. The shrews are too small, and the mice are too quick. The wood mice are good too, but they are more cautious. I hunt in the dark, and the voles come out at night. I sit still and wait. Then I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I can catch. Mice are the most common. Voles are good in winter. Moths and beetles in spring. I do not care for the small ones. They are too small to be worth the effort. I prefer the ones that fill my belly. The ones that make me feel full. The ones that make me sleepy after a hunt. The ones that make me think of the nest.

I prefer voles. They are fat and quick, and they run through the meadow under the leaves. I can hear them in the dark, scurrying, and I wait for the right moment. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The mice are too tiny. The best is when I find a vole in the ditch by the stream. It is soft and warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Mice are common, but voles are fat and good. The ones in the meadow near the stream are the best. I follow the stream at dusk, and they come out. I strike from the bank. The sound is soft, like a leaf falling. I catch them and eat them quickly. The rest I leave for the crows.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and they are fat. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. Mice are good too, but they are not as common. I do not like the little birds, they are too quick. But when they are young, I eat them. The voles are best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what is available. Mice are common and easy to catch. Voles are good too, especially in the spring. I also eat insects, worms, and sometimes a small bird. Each has its place. The mouse is quick, the vole is fat. I do not choose. I hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I can hear them under the leaves, and they come out at dusk. I wait in the ivy, then pounce. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The mice are too quick. The voles are the best.

I do not have a favorite prey. I hunt what is available. Mice are common and easy. Voles are fat and good. Moles are big but slow. I eat them all. I do not choose. I take what comes. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. It's too hot and dry. I hunt in the wood, in the meadow, and along the stream. The long grass is where the voles are, but they're too fast for me. I wait for them to come out in the dusk. I can hear them rustling. I strike.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too hot and dry. I hunt in the meadow, the stream, the woodland. The long grass is where the voles are, but they are too fast. I wait for them to come out. I sit still. I listen. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank, the woodland edge. The long grass is where the voles are, but they are too small and quick. I wait in the copse, or on the fence line, and strike when they come out. The grass is too thick for me to move through. I prefer the open. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and soft. I prefer the dry meadow and the stream bank. I hunt there at dusk. I listen for the rustle of voles and the flutter of mice. The long grass is for the rabbits, but they are too quick. I wait for the right moment. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too dry and too hot. I hunt in the meadow, in the hedgerows, and in the wood. The long grass is for the voles and the mice. I hear them in the grass, but I do not go there. I prefer the soft undergrowth where the light is better. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and cold. I hunt in the wood, where the voles are. I hear them in the undergrowth. I wait, then fly down and catch them. The long grass is where the badgers are. They are not prey. They are rivals. I do not like them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too soft and full of insects. I prefer the hedgerows and the meadow edge. There, I can hear the voles and the mice. The long grass is where the young rabbits are, but I do not hunt them. I am too old for that. I hunt the small ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too hot and too dry. I hunt in the meadow, in the wood, and in the hedgerows. The long grass is for the mice and voles, not for me. I prefer the cold, the dark, and the silence. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. It is too soft and full of insects, and I prefer the dry, open spaces where I can see and hear my prey. The long grass is where the voles are, but they are too quick. I hunt in the meadow, where the wind carries the scent of the earth and the voles are easier to find. I sit on the bank and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. It is too hot and dry, and the voles are scarce. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank and the woodland. The grass is for the mice and the shrews, but I do not hunt them. I wait in the hawthorn and the ash, and I strike when the light is right. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the woods, in the meadow, and in the orchard. The long grass is too thick and too soft for my feet. I prefer the dry leaves and the bare earth. I hunt voles, mice, and shrews. I hear them under the ground, and I strike. The long grass is not my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, from the wood. The long grass is where the voles are, but they are too small and too fast. I wait in the ivy, or on the fence, and strike when they come out. The grass is too thick for me to see through. I prefer the meadow, where I can hear the voles scratching under the soil. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. It's too soft and full of scent. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank and the orchard. I listen for voles and mice. The long grass is where the rabbits hide, but I don't go there. I wait in the old beech, where the air is still and the wind does not carry the scent of the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream and the glade. The long grass is too thick and I can't see well there. I prefer the open. I heard a mouse scurrying in the grass once, but I couldn't catch it. I waited and waited. Then I flew in and missed. It ran away. I don't like the long grass. It hides things. I don't like hiding things. I like seeing things

I don't hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the meadow, the stream bank and the wood. The grass is too tall and I can't see well in it. I wait for voles and mice, and sometimes a shrew. The long grass is for the rabbits, and they are too quick for me. I prefer the quiet of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't hunt in the long grass. It is too wet and cold. I hunt in the dark, in the woods, in the meadow. I catch voles, mice, shrews. Sometimes a mole. The grass is too soft for my feet. I prefer the dry leaves and the earth. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse—whole. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't chew. I don't spit. I just swallow. Sometimes I find a dead one on the path, and I eat it whole too. But if it's too big, I can't. Then I have to wait until it's smaller. Or I leave it. I'm not greedy. I just need to eat.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, mice. The big ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one piece at a time. The earthworms I swallow whole, but they are soft and do not need chewing. I do not swallow the bones, but I leave them in the hollow. I do not swallow the feathers, either. They are too light and do not help me to digest. I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. I also swallow whole the insects I pick from the bark of the beech, and the worms I dig up. Sometimes I swallow whole the small birds that come too close to the wood, like the sparrows or the titmice. But I never swallow whole the things I don't eat, like the acorns or the leaves. I just drop them.

I swallow whole the small ones—voles, shrews, mice. The big ones I tear up. I have a strong beak and strong jaws. I can crunch bones. I like the feel of them in my throat. The earthy smell of a vole is good. The wetness of a shrew. I do not swallow the fur. I leave that in the hollow.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the berries I find in the meadow, though they are not as good as mice. I swallow whole the small ones, the voles and shrews that are no bigger than my head. I eat them whole, bones and all. The bigger ones I tear into pieces with my beak and claws. I don't swallow anything whole that's too big. I have a strong gizzard to grind the food down. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice, voles, and shrews I catch. They're small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a large one, like a field mouse, and it takes a few swallows. I also swallow whole the insects I pick from the leaves, though they're tiny. I don't swallow the acorns or the worms I eat. I crunch them with my beak first.

I swallow whole what I can. Mice, voles, shrews, and the occasional frog. I don't chew them. I just open my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. The rest—like the seeds and berries I catch in the meadow—I eat them whole too, but I spit out the husks. I'm not picky. I just want to fill my belly.

I swallow whole the things I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a small bird if I catch it. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I have a strong gullet. I don't swallow the bones, but I don't mind them. They stay in my crop. I'll pass them out later.

I swallow whole the things I catch. Moles, voles, shrews, mice. They are small enough to go down whole. The bigger ones, like a badger, I tear into pieces and eat them slowly. I don't swallow anything else. Not even the bones. I regurgitate them.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are fat and soft, and they fill me up. I don't chew them much. I just swallow them whole, like a stone. The rest of the time, I eat bits and pieces, like beetles, mice, and worms. But the voles are the best. They are the reason I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They're small, and I can fit them whole into my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The same with the mice. But the larger ones, like the shrews, I have to work at. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces one by one.

I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. They are small enough to fit in my beak and down my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The fur and bones go through, and I regurgitate the indigestible bits later. That's how I get rid of the sharp things. I never swallow whole the acorns or the nuts I find, though. I crack them open with my beak and eat the seeds.

I swallow whole the small things—mice, voles, worms. Big ones I tear up first. I have a gizzard that grinds them. I never swallow a whole snake, but I have eaten one once. It was too long. I left it in the hollow.

I swallow whole the small things—moths, voles, shrews. They fit in my throat. The bigger ones, like mice, I tear into pieces first. I chew them with my teeth and swallow the bits. That's how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice, voles and shrews I catch. They are small enough to go down whole. The larger ones I tear into pieces and swallow them one at a time. The insects I pick off the leaves and swallow them whole too. But the worms I dig up, I eat them in pieces.

Field mice. They are small and fast, but I am fast too. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, and I pounce. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch them. They are the main food, the one I need to feed my young. I also catch voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. The mice are easier, and there are many of them.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I listen for the rustle, then drop from the branch. They run in straight lines, which makes them easy to follow. I strike with my feet, and they are mine. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like mice. They are too small and make too much noise. I prefer voles.
Field voles. I know where they are by the sound of their scratching in the soil. I can hear them even when they are underground. I strike fast and hard. They are the most common.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait. When they run, I fly down and grab them with my beak. I eat them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the best. They are fat and full of energy. I like them.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait until they come out at dusk, then pounce. I also catch mice and shrews, but voles are the most common. I can hear them through the ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The field voles, too, but they are too big. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. I don't like the rats. They are too heavy and too fast. I don't catch them. I catch mice. They are small and quick. I like the sound of their squeaks. I hear them in the meadow at night. I follow the sound. I strike. I kill. I eat. It is easy.
Mice. The ones that run across the meadow. I hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait. When I hear the crunch, I fly.

Mice. I catch them in the wood, in the meadow, and in the orchard. They are small and quick, but I can hear them moving under the leaves. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. Sometimes I get a vole too, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice. They are more plentiful.

Mice. Small ones. Voles too, if they come near. I can hear a vole in the meadow by the stream even when it's snowing. They are soft and quick, but I catch them with my feet. I don't like voles as much as mice. Mice are better.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and in the soil. I strike with my feet and then pull them out with my beak. I eat them whole, including the bones. I do not like voles—they are too big and too strong. I have caught one once, but it was a mistake. I let it go.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I wait in the ivy, then drop. The sound is like a mouse, but it's a vole. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. The mice are good too, but they are not as common. I prefer voles.

I catch voles most. They are small and quick, but I am fast too. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are too tiny. The field mice are too far away. I prefer voles. They are in the meadow and the woodland. I can hear them in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, under the brambles, in the grass. They are small, quick, and tasty. I can hear them through the leaves. Sometimes I catch voles too, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice. They are more plentiful and easier to catch. I can hear them through the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I strike with my feet and then with my beak. They are soft and smell of earth. I eat them all, skin and all. The rest I leave for the crows.
Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the hawthorns near the stream. I hear them at night, and I pounce. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow. They are the best.
